```{r setup, include = FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,

```

Many animals search for food by moving slowly and tortuously where they find
it, and fast and straight between such places: area-restricted search (ARS).
The first passage time (FPT) is the time an animal takes to cross a circle of
a given radius centred on one of its locations (Fauchald & Tveraa 2003). It is
long within a patch and short between patches, so its variance among locations
is largest for circles about the size of the patches. The radius at which the
variance of the log FPT peaks is taken as the scale of ARS.

`tidytracks` provides:

- `event_fpt()`: the FPT of each location, for one radius;
- `track_fpt_profile()`: the variance of the log FPT of each track for a set
  of radii (the profile), plotted with `autoplot()`;
- `track_suggest_ars_scale()`: the radius of the peak of each profile.

This article applies them to four African buffalo, explains the defaults, and
lists the options to try with other data.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(tidytracks)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Data

We use the GPS tracks of four African buffalo (*Syncerus caffer*) from Kruger
National Park, South Africa (Getz et al. 2007, Cross et al. 2016), also used in
the article "Movement models with ctmm". Cilla, Gabs and Mvubu were located
every hour; Pepper every hour, then every two hours, which also affects its FPT
(see Options). The FPT is computed on the plane, so we project the tracks with
an azimuthal equidistant projection centred on the study area:

```{r load_data}
buffalo_tt <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/buffalo_tracks.csv",
  col_track_id = "buffalo_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time"
) %>%
  sf::st_transform("+proj=aeqd +lat_0=-25 +lon_0=31.8 +units=m") %>%
  tt_order_time()
buffalo_tt
```

## FPT of each location

`event_fpt()` returns the FPT of each location for one radius (here 3 km), in
hours. Locations near the ends of a track get `NA`, as the track does not
leave the circle on both sides.

```{r event_fpt}
buffalo_tt <- buffalo_tt %>%
  mutate(fpt_3km = event_fpt(buffalo_tt, as_units(3, "km")))
summary(as.numeric(buffalo_tt$fpt_3km))
```

A buffalo stays for days in some areas, and crosses others in hours:

```{r map_fpt}
ggplot(filter(buffalo_tt, buffalo_id == "Cilla")) +
  geom_sf(aes(colour = as.numeric(fpt_3km)), size = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(trans = "log10", na.value = "grey80") +
  labs(colour = "FPT (h)\nat 3 km")
```

## Profiles and scale of ARS

`track_fpt_profile()` computes the variance of the log FPT of each track at
50 radii:

```{r profile}
profile <- track_fpt_profile(buffalo_tt)
profile
autoplot(profile) + facet_wrap(~id)
```

`track_suggest_ars_scale()` returns the radius of the highest peak of each
profile:

```{r suggest}
scales <- track_suggest_ars_scale(profile, units = as_units("km"))
scales
```

All four profiles have a peak, at
`r round(min(as.numeric(scales)), 1)`–`r round(max(as.numeric(scales)), 1)`
km; Cilla's has a second, almost as high, at about 7 km. The variance is also
high at the smallest radii, which a buffalo crosses quickly when it walks and
slowly when it rests; this end of a profile is not a peak, as a peak must be
higher than the radii on both sides. Inspect the profiles before using a
suggested scale: not all species use ARS, and a profile without a clear peak
(e.g. declining steadily) has no scale of ARS, even if noise gives it small
peaks.

## Default radii

Two ranges of radii are not informative:

- **Radii within a step.** If a circle is smaller than the steps before and
  after a location, the track crosses it on these steps, and the FPT is
  proportional to the radius, by a factor set by their speed. The variance of
  the log FPT then measures the variation in speed, whatever the radius. This matters most for long steps
  (e.g. one location every few hours) and large location errors.
- **Radii larger than about half the extent of a track.** A location has an
  FPT only if the track goes farther than the radius from it both before and
  after it. As the radius grows, fewer locations have an FPT, and these are
  the locations far from the ends of the track.

By default, each track therefore gets 50 radii, evenly spaced on a log scale,
from twice the median distance between its consecutive locations to half the
diagonal of its bounding box. The column `n_valid` of the profile gives the
number of locations with an FPT. With radii up to 62 km, the diagonal of the
bounding box of the largest track (Pepper's), the largest radii have none:

```{r n_valid}
profile_wide <- track_fpt_profile(
  buffalo_tt,
  radii = as_units(exp(seq(log(0.1), log(62), length.out = 50)), "km")
)
ggplot(profile_wide, aes(x = as.numeric(radius), y = n_valid)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = buffalo_id)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Radius (km)", y = "Locations with an FPT", colour = "Buffalo") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Radii with enough locations

Where the number of locations with an FPT falls steeply, the variance can
jump. A radius is therefore used only if at least half of the locations of the
track have an FPT at it (by default; argument `min_prop_valid`, column
`enough_events`).
`autoplot()` draws the other radii with dashed lines, and
`track_suggest_ars_scale()` ignores them.

The profile of Mvubu has a peak at 3 km, and a spike near the end of its
range of radii. If radii with few locations are used, the spike becomes the
highest peak:

```{r min_prop_valid}
profile_all <- track_fpt_profile(buffalo_tt, min_prop_valid = 0.01)
scales_all <- track_suggest_ars_scale(profile_all, units = as_units("km"))
scales_all
autoplot(filter(profile, buffalo_id == "Mvubu")) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1000 * as.numeric(c(scales["Mvubu"], scales_all["Mvubu"])),
    linetype = c("solid", "dotted"),
    colour = "darkred"
  )
```

In the default profile (above), the spike (dotted line) is at the last radius
with enough locations, so it is not a peak (a peak must be higher than the
radii on both sides), and the peak at 3 km (solid line) is selected.

## Highest or first peak

A profile can have several peaks. By default, `track_suggest_ars_scale()`
returns the highest (`method = "max"`). The first peak (`method = "first"`) can
be a small bump before the main peak, as for Pepper:

```{r method}
scales_first <- track_suggest_ars_scale(
  profile,
  method = "first",
  units = as_units("km")
)
scales_first
autoplot(filter(profile, buffalo_id == "Pepper")) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1000 * as.numeric(c(scales_first["Pepper"], scales["Pepper"])),
    linetype = c("dotted", "solid"),
    colour = "darkred"
  )
```

Animals can search at nested scales (e.g. patches within larger areas), so a
first peak can be meaningful; the profile shows whether it is.

## Options

- **Radii:** `radii` sets the radii, as a `units` object (e.g. from what is
  known of the species), for all tracks. `autoplot()` then also draws the
  median profile. Radii evenly spaced on a log scale give the same detail at
  all scales:

  ```{r radii, eval = FALSE}
  radii <- as_units(exp(seq(log(0.5), log(20), length.out = 40)), "km")
  track_fpt_profile(buffalo_tt, radii = radii)
  ```

- **Locations per radius:** `min_prop_valid` (0.5 by default) is the
  proportion of the locations of a track that must have an FPT at a radius. A
  lower value keeps more large radii, with more noise.
- **Peak:** `method` selects the highest peak (`"max"`, the default), the
  first (`"first"`), or the one around which the variance changes most
  (`"steep"`). `peak_width` (1 by default) is the number of radii on either
  side of a peak that must not have a higher variance; larger values ignore
  narrow peaks. The peaks of the buffalo are broad, so here the scales do not
  change:

  ```{r peak_width}
  track_suggest_ars_scale(profile, peak_width = 3, units = as_units("km"))
  ```

- **Groups:** if the tibble is grouped by a column of its events (e.g. the
  season), the log FPTs of each group are pooled into one profile; the FPT is
  still computed on whole tracks. For central place foragers, split the tracks
  into trips with `tt_split_trips()`, so that the time between trips does not
  count, and group the trips by animal.
- **Sampling:** the FPT depends on the sampling interval. Regularise tracks
  with `tt_regular_time()` if it varies, and compare tracks with similar
  sampling.
- **Kernel bandwidth:** the scale can inform the bandwidth of `hr_tt_kde()`.
  The bandwidth is the standard deviation of a Gaussian kernel, not a radius:
  a kernel with a bandwidth equal to the radius has 39% of its mass within
  it, and 95% within 2.45 times it.
